roadmaps.tagline: TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Accenture, Cognizant, Capgemini
roadmaps.summary: The shortest honest path to clearing a mass-recruiter drive. These companies test breadth, not depth: clean basics, steady coding, aptitude, and the confidence to explain what you wrote. Work through this in order and you will have seen every shape of question they ask.
roadmaps.forWho: Pre-final and final year students sitting for campus drives.

milestones.title: Write and run programs without hesitating
milestones.why: Every drive starts with a timed online round. Fumbling over input parsing or a for-loop costs you the questions you could have solved.

milestones.title: Arrays
milestones.why: More campus coding questions are array questions than anything else: traversal, searching, rotation, sub-arrays.

milestones.title: Strings
milestones.why: Palindromes, anagrams, reversal, counting characters. Cheap marks once you stop fearing index arithmetic.

milestones.title: Searching and sorting
milestones.why: Binary search turns a brute-force timeout into a pass. Knowing which sort to reach for is routinely asked aloud in interviews.

milestones.title: Hashing
milestones.why: The single highest-leverage idea in this list: it collapses most nested-loop solutions into one pass.

milestones.title: Two pointers and sliding window
milestones.why: The two patterns that come up whenever a question says subarray, pair, or without repeating characters.

milestones.title: Stacks, queues and linked lists
milestones.why: Rarely the hard question, often the viva question. You are expected to be able to draw one and code one.

milestones.title: Recursion and introductory DP
milestones.why: Fibonacci, staircase, coin change. Service companies stop about here, so a working memoised solution is enough.

milestones.title: Aptitude and logical reasoning
milestones.why: The round most people lose, because they practise code and assume aptitude will take care of itself. It will not: it is timed arithmetic under pressure.

milestones.title: Company-pattern practice
milestones.why: Each recruiter has habits. Sit the company sets closest to your drive once you can already solve the topics above.

milestones.title: Explain your own code out loud
milestones.why: The technical interview is mostly walk me through what you did. Re-open three problems you solved and narrate the approach, the complexity, and one case you got wrong first.

roadmaps.summary: Java is still what most Indian service and product companies build on. This path takes you from syntax to a deployable Spring Boot service, with the data-structure work that interviews actually test sitting alongside it rather than after it.
roadmaps.forWho: Students targeting Java backend roles, or anyone whose college stack is Java.

milestones.title: Java syntax and your first programs
milestones.why: Types, loops, methods, and reading input. Nothing here is interesting, and everything later depends on it.

milestones.title: Arrays and strings
milestones.why: A Java String is immutable and a Java array is fixed-length. Both facts shape how you solve almost every question.

milestones.title: Object-oriented programming
milestones.why: Classes, inheritance, interfaces, polymorphism. This is the part of the interview where a wrong answer is remembered.

milestones.title: Collections framework
milestones.why: List, Set, Map, and when each one is the right answer. Being able to describe HashMap is close to mandatory.

milestones.title: Exceptions and file I/O
milestones.why: Checked versus unchecked, try-with-resources, and reading a file without leaking a handle.

milestones.title: Linked lists, stacks and queues
milestones.why: Implement them once by hand. After that you will understand what the library is doing for you.

milestones.title: Trees and graphs
milestones.why: Traversals, depth, and the two searches. Where product-company interviews start and service-company ones usually stop.

milestones.title: Dynamic programming
milestones.why: Recognising overlapping subproblems. Aim for a correct memo table before you chase elegance.

milestones.title: SQL and databases
milestones.why: Every backend role asks for joins, grouping and an index. It is the most reliably examined non-Java topic in a Java interview.

milestones.title: Spring Boot and REST APIs
milestones.why: Controllers, dependency injection, and a service that answers on a port. This is what the job is.

reading.label: Spring: Building a RESTful Web Service

milestones.title: Ship one project, then prepare to defend it
milestones.why: A small, finished, deployed service beats three half-built ones. Be ready to explain every dependency you added.

roadmaps.summary: Analyst roles reward a different skill from software roles: getting a messy table into a shape that answers a question, and then saying what it means. Python and SQL are the tools; the judgement is the job.
roadmaps.forWho: Students aiming at data analyst, BI or junior data science roles.

milestones.title: Python basics
milestones.why: Loops, functions, conditionals, input. Get fluent enough that the language stops being the obstacle.

milestones.title: Lists, dictionaries and sets
milestones.why: Almost all data cleaning is dictionary work in disguise. Counting and grouping by hand first will make pandas make sense later.

milestones.title: Strings and text handling
milestones.why: Real data arrives dirty: trailing spaces, mixed case, inconsistent separators. Text wrangling is most of the work.

milestones.title: Sorting, searching and slicing
milestones.why: Top-N, ranking and lookups are the questions analysts are actually asked, every week.

milestones.title: Recursion and problem decomposition
milestones.why: Less for the interview than for the habit: break a question into a smaller version of itself before writing anything.

milestones.title: NumPy and pandas
milestones.why: DataFrames, filtering, groupby, merge. The point where you stop writing loops over rows.

milestones.title: SQL for analysis
milestones.why: This is the round you will be tested on. Joins, GROUP BY, then window functions, in that order.

milestones.title: Statistics you will be asked about
milestones.why: Mean versus median and why it matters, distributions, correlation is not causation, and what a p-value does and does not say.

milestones.title: Visualisation and explaining a result
milestones.why: A chart that needs explaining has failed. Practise reducing a finding to one sentence and one picture.

milestones.title: One end-to-end analysis
milestones.why: Take a public dataset, ask a real question, clean it, chart it, and write the answer in a paragraph. That is your portfolio.

roadmaps.summary: The fastest route to something you can show someone. You build visible things early, which keeps motivation up, but the fundamentals still decide whether you pass the interview, so they stay in the path rather than being skipped.
roadmaps.forWho: Students aiming at frontend, full-stack or product-engineering roles.

milestones.title: Programming foundations
milestones.why: Frameworks change every two years. Loops, functions and conditionals do not.

milestones.title: HTML and CSS
milestones.why: Semantic markup, the box model, flexbox and grid. Most of the frustration here is one unread page of documentation.

milestones.title: JavaScript fundamentals
milestones.why: Arrays and strings are where JavaScript is actually written: map, filter, reduce, split, join.

milestones.title: The DOM and browser APIs
milestones.why: Events, fetch, and local storage. Enough to make a page respond to a person without any framework at all.

milestones.title: Data structures behind the UI
milestones.why: Hash maps for lookups, stacks for undo and history. Interviews ask these even for frontend roles.

milestones.title: Git and the command line
milestones.why: Branch, commit, merge, resolve a conflict. Not optional, and quietly assessed from your first day.

milestones.title: React
milestones.why: Components, state and props. Learn why re-renders happen before learning the hooks that work around them.

milestones.title: Node and REST APIs
milestones.why: A server, a route, a JSON response. Once your own frontend talks to your own backend, full-stack stops being a buzzword.

milestones.title: Databases
milestones.why: Store something that survives a restart. Schemas, queries, and why you never concatenate user input into SQL.

milestones.title: Algorithms for the interview round
milestones.why: Even frontend interviews include one coding question. Two pointers, searching and a little recursion cover most of them.

milestones.title: Deploy it, then write about it
milestones.why: A live URL and a readable README are worth more than a private repository with twice the code.
